results.summary: This design implements a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron network inspired by snnTorch. It accepts an 8-bit input current split between two input neurons, and each neuron integrates the current, decays its state by bit-shifting each clock cycle, and emits a spike when its state reaches or exceeds a threshold of 8. The network has multiple layers, with spike outputs for each layer and state variable outputs for the output layer neurons. The documentation provides no testing procedure or external hardware requirements, and the design is a compact digital implementation of a spiking neural network building block.

This project is a 4-bit up/down binary counter with enable and test mode. It uses input pins for test, up/down selection, and enable, and outputs the 4-bit count value. Testing requires connecting the enable pin to VDD, test to GND, up/down to a switch, reset to an RC startup circuit, and a 50 MHz clock, with the outputs connected to LEDs. The design is a straightforward digital building block with minimal documentation beyond basic operation.

This design implements the control block for an 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture. It uses a 6-stage sequential counter and a lookup table to generate control signals from a 4-bit opcode, with outputs for various register and memory control lines as well as a halt signal. Testing involves applying opcodes and monitoring the control signal outputs, optionally using a logic analyzer or slowing the clock. The project is part of a course (ECE 298A) and is intended to be integrated with other CPU sub-blocks.

This is a simple analog switch that connects or disconnects two analog pins (X and Y) based on a digital control input. When the control input is high, X and Y are connected; when low, they are isolated. The design also provides an inverse of the control signal as a digital output. Testing involves applying a digital high to X, a pull-down resistor on Y, and toggling the control input to verify connectivity and the inverse output.

CORA-16 is a 16-bit CPU that uses external SPI memory for instruction fetch and execution. It features a byte-wide general-purpose input and output bus, and supports single-stepping for debugging via a step pin. Status pins indicate busy, halt, and trap conditions, with trap recovery possible by stepping. The design requires an external SPI RAM, such as a Raspberry Pi acting as an emulator, to load and run programs.

This project implements a 4x4 structural array multiplier using full adders and AND gates. It takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product. The design is built from basic logic gates and full adders, forming partial products and summing them with carry propagation. It is an educational project (ECE-UY 2204) intended to demonstrate digital arithmetic design, and testing involves applying input values and comparing the output to expected results.

This design implements an 8-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit for unsigned integers using Vedic multipliers and reversible gates. Inputs are registered on half a clock cycle, and the MAC operation is performed with the multiplier and adder each taking half a clock cycle. The result is output on dedicated and bidirectional pins. The project explores reversible gates for energy efficiency and requires no external hardware.

This design implements a delta recurrent neural network (Delta RNN) combined with a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron. It accepts an 8-bit input current, computes the difference between previous and current states, and generates a spike when that difference exceeds a set delta threshold. Outputs include the state variable and the difference in states. The documentation provides no testing procedure or external hardware requirements, and the design is a compact digital implementation of a spiking neural network component.

This project runs the main peripherals of a Basys 3 FPGA board over a 115200 baud UART link. It handles 16 LED inputs, 16 switch outputs, 12 seven-segment display inputs, and 5 button outputs, all communicated via UART TX and RX routed to the bidirectional PMOD bus. Testing can be done with an associated PMOD board or by interacting with the UART, expecting messages like "LD: 0xFFFF" and "SW: 0xFFFF". The design enables remote control of Basys 3 peripherals through a serial connection.

This project implements a 16-byte RAM built from D flip-flops. It supports read and write operations with a 4-bit address, active-low chip enable and load signals, and an 8-bit data input. Read operations are asynchronous, and the output is high-impedance when not enabled. The design is intended for integration into an 8-bit processor and includes CocoTB testbenches that verify write and read functionality across all addresses.
